title: Trust thyself
hookLine: Emerson's Self-Reliance: every heart vibrates to that iron string, trust thyself
carry: give my own inner gleam a fair hearing

cards: A meeting. Someone across the table makes a point, and everybody nods. It's good.

It's exactly right. And at the end of the table, someone else goes quiet, because the same thought crossed their mind earlier, and they let it go. It seemed too obvious, or too odd, or not quite their place to say.

Now it belongs to somebody else. Emerson starts his essay Self-Reliance very near that moment, and builds a whole philosophy out of it. A little further on come two words, set down like a bell rung once: trust thyself.

teach.b: First, the rejected thought. Near the start of Self-Reliance, Emerson writes: "In every work of genius we recognize our own rejected thoughts: they come back to us with a certain alienated majesty."
Your own idea, coming back grand and strange, wearing someone else's name. We dismiss our own thoughts, he says, simply because they're ours. Second, the gleam.
A person should learn to watch for the gleam of light that flashes across the mind from within, more than the brilliance of all the poets and sages. Not instead of them. More than them.
The books matter, but the flash is yours, and only you can catch it. Third, the iron string.

"Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string." A string pulled tight, and when it's struck, every heart hums with it. The call to self-trust isn't strange or rare, Emerson says; everyone already feels it.
Fourth, what it does not mean. Despite the title, the essay isn't mainly about money, or never asking for help. And trust here isn't stubbornness, or doing whatever you feel like.
It's quieter: giving your own honest perception a fair hearing before you hand it over to the crowd.
The quiet thought at the end of that table may have been wrong. But nobody found out, because it wasn't trusted long enough to be said.

how: Some readers of Self-Reliance take 'trust thyself' as a call to give their own honest perception a fair hearing, alongside books and other people's opinions rather than beneath them.

o: always do whatever you happen to feel like
give your own honest thoughts a fair hearing
never take advice or help from anyone else

games.q: inside trust thyself: tap the pairs.
p: flashes across the mind from within

s: Self-Reliance is mainly about money and never asking for help
despite the title, it's about trusting your own honest perception.
Emerson says we dismiss our own thoughts because they're ours
then they come back to us in someone else's work, with a certain alienated majesty.
Emerson says to ignore poets and sages
he says to watch the gleam from within more than them, not instead of them.

games.q: a thought flashes across your mind in a meeting. it seems too obvious to say. what does Emerson's essay suggest?
o: let it go; someone smarter will say it.
give it a fair hearing and say it.
write it down and never mention it.
games.why: Emerson warns that otherwise we'll hear our own thought from someone else, coming back with a certain alienated majesty.

practice: Let your mind go quiet enough to notice what comes up on its own: somewhere in there is a small, steady knowing you've been talking yourself out of, something to start, something to stop, someone to call.
You don't have to act on it; just let it be heard all the way through, without the usual voice that says, who are you to think that?

wordCard.voice: Trust thyself. Emerson's two words from Self-Reliance: give your own honest perception a fair hearing, because every heart, he says, vibrates to that iron string. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: give my own inner gleam a fair hearing. Not stubbornness, just a fair hearing. Back tomorrow, same hill.
